[0] Austin, Texas (AP) — Local police said a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer shot and wounded a man in the Texas capital Austin on Sunday afternoon, prompting anti-ICE demonstrators to quickly gather at the scene.

[1] Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said at a press conference attended by the mayor and other city officials that the unidentified man was shot once in the torso in the north of the city and was in serious but stable condition after being taken to hospital.

[2] The Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, did not send anyone to the press conference and did not immediately respond to requests for details.

[3] Davis told reporters that Austin police were not involved in the enforcement operation or the shooting, which followed a vehicle stop.

[4] Democratic Austin Mayor Watson said she wanted the city's police force to take part so as to provide "clear, third-party" oversight during the investigation. Watson said it would not be appropriate for ICE to investigate itself.

[5] Watson noted that Austin residents "have the right to feel safe in the city they live in" and added that a proper investigation would only make the outcome more credible.

[6] Davis said she did not yet know the nationality of the man who was shot. She noted that not long after the incident she had few details to offer, but stressed that her special investigations unit had been dispatched to the scene.

[7] Local media reported that a dark-blue Toyota Corolla was parked beneath an overpass, with damage to the passenger side of the car that appeared to be bullet holes.

[8] A large number of law enforcement officers were on scene, and about a hundred demonstrators also gathered. Some protesters shouted at officers holding riot shields, while others shouted at passing vehicles, drawing supportive honks from drivers. One man held a placard reading "No one is safe"; another read "ICE Nazis".

[9] When asked whether Austin authorities knew the whereabouts of the federal agent involved (since in past similar shootings in other states the agent had left the area), the mayor replied: "We don't know. But I hope the agent involved in the shooting will not leave the city, and certainly should not leave the state."

[10] Democratic US Representative Castiel, who represents parts of Austin, called on authorities to remain transparent in their investigation of the shooting.

[11] Castiel told reporters: "It is heartbreaking that such a horror has come to my doorstep. For Austin to truly be safe, ICE must stop its sweep operations here."

[12] The shooting came as ICE has been stepping up enforcement across the country this summer, with monthly arrests in July and August each surpassing 50,000 — a record for the agency.

[13] In July, an ICE agent in Houston shot and killed 52-year-old Sergio Arellano Jr. (Salgado Araujo) during a pursuit; federal agents in an unmarked vehicle had been tailing Arellano, who was driving construction workers to a job site.

[14] In July, in Maine, a 25-year-old Colombian man, John Sebastian, was shot by an ICE agent. The agent, a US Army veteran, suffered from severe mental health issues from childhood and should never have been issued a badge and a gun to patrol US streets, several close relatives told the AP.

[15] The agency's enforcement operations drew widespread condemnation last winter following the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota.

[16] ___

[17] Webber reported from Los Angeles. AP reporters Rebecca Boone (Boise, Idaho), Kimberly Kruesi (Providence, Rhode Island) and Tim Sullivan (Minneapolis) contributed to this report.
